---
title: "Coming from statnet, sna, and network"
description: >
  A function-by-function map from sna and network to knappnet, how sna's
  matrix-based conventions carry over, and QAP compared with qaptest() and
  netlm().
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

[sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) works on adjacency matrices (or `network` objects, which it turns into
matrices), and its results follow from that: parallel edges collapse into
one tie, the diagonal is ignored by default, and a node's score is the
row of a matrix computation. knappnet works on a node table and an edge
table, and by default follows [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s conventions, which differ from
sna's in a few places. One argument, `convention = "sna"`, reproduces
sna's choices exactly, and the QAP functions follow sna's conventions for
dyads, missing values, and p-values.

Every knappnet function starts with `net_` (`net_degree()`,
`net_betweenness()`, `net_closeness()`, `net_components()`,
`net_brokerage()`), so none masks sna's `degree()` or `betweenness()`.
This article still calls sna and network with `sna::` and `network::` so
that every line says which package computes it.

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## Converting

`as_net_frame()` reads a `network` object, and `net_to_network()` converts
back, keeping vertex, edge, and network attributes. For bipartite
networks a `mode` node column records the two sets. Matrices work in both
directions too:

```{r}
# Padgett's Florentine marriage ties, with the Pucci family added as an
# isolate (it married outside this group); see ?net_example.
ties <- net_example("florentine")$edges
families <- data.frame(name = sort(unique(c(ties$source, ties$target, "Pucci"))))
flo <- net_frame(ties, nodes = families, directed = FALSE, id = "name")

net <- net_to_network(flo)
network::network.size(net)
network::network.edgecount(net)
as_net_frame(net)

m <- as.matrix(flo)   # a symmetric 0/1 sociomatrix with node names
m[1:4, 1:4]
```

These are Padgett's Florentine marriage ties (Breiger and Pattison 1986);
the Pucci family has no marriage ties in the data and is an isolate.

## Function map

`gmode = "graph"` in [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) corresponds to `directed = FALSE` on the
net_frame; the network itself says whether it is directed, so knappnet
functions have no `gmode`.

| sna / network | knappnet | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `network(m, directed)`, `as.network()` | `net_frame(edges, nodes, directed)`, `as_net_frame(m)` | |
| `as.sociomatrix(net)`, `as.matrix(net)` | `as.matrix(g)` | Parallel edges are summed; `attr` fills the matrix with an edge column. |
| `network.size()`, `network.edgecount()` | `nrow(g$nodes)`, `nrow(g$edges)` | |
| `get.vertex.attribute(net, "x")` | `g$nodes$x` | |
| `degree(m, cmode = "freeman")` | `net_degree(g)` | Total degree, in plus out, in directed networks. |
| `degree(m, cmode = "indegree" / "outdegree")` | `net_degree(g, mode = "in" / "out")` | |
| any sna measure on a network with loops or repeated ties | the same measure with `convention = "sna"` | Parallel edges collapse into one tie and loops are ignored, as when the network is a sociomatrix. |
| `betweenness(m, gmode, cmode)` | `net_betweenness(g, convention = "sna")` | Identical on networks without parallel edges. sna's `rescale = TRUE` is `b / sum(b)`. |
| `closeness(m, gmode, cmode)` | `net_closeness(g, convention = "sna")` | sna gives 0 to every node that cannot reach all others; see below. |
| `closeness(m, cmode = "suminvdir" / "suminvundir")` | `net_harmonic(g, convention = "sna")` | Divided by n - 1. |
| `evcent(m, gmode)` | `net_eigen(g, convention = "sna")` | Unit Euclidean norm; out-ties in directed networks. |
| `gden(m, diag = FALSE)` | `net_density(g, convention = "sna")` | |
| `centralization(m, degree)`, `betweenness`, `closeness` | `net_centralization(g, measure, convention = "sna")` | sna's theoretical maxima, which differ from [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s for degree. |
| `components(m, connected)`, `component.dist()` | `net_components(g, mode)`, `net_fragmentation(g, mode)` | sna defaults to strong components (`connected = "strong"`); knappnet to weak. |
| `kcores(m)` | `net_coreness(g)` | |
| `clique.census(m)` | `net_max_cliques(g)`, `net_clique_number(g)` | knappnet lists the maximal cliques themselves. |
| `triad.census(m, mode = "digraph")` | `net_triad_census(g)` | Identical on directed networks. For undirected data sna reports four classes, knappnet all sixteen with every tie mutual. |
| `brokerage(m, cl)$raw.nli` | `net_brokerage(g, groups)` | Columns `w_I`, `w_O`, `b_IO`, `b_OI`, `b_O`, `t` are `coordinator`, `itinerant`, `representative`, `gatekeeper`, `liaison`, `total`. |
| `sedist(m, method)` | `net_struct_equiv(g, method)` | sna's default method is `"hamming"`, knappnet's `"euclidean"`. Same treatment of the diagonal (`diag = FALSE`). |
| `equiv.clust(m)` | `hclust(as.dist(net_struct_equiv(g)))` | |
| (concoR package) | `net_concor(g, depth)` | |
| `gcor(y, x)` | `net_qap_cor(y, x)$statistic` | Identical. |
| `qaptest(list(y, x), gcor, g1 = 1, g2 = 2)` | `net_qap_cor(y, x)` | Same reference distribution; `exact = TRUE` enumerates every permutation. |
| `netlm(y, x, nullhyp = "qap")` | `net_mrqap(y, x)` | Double semi-partialling (Dekker et al. 2007), sna's default. |
| `netlm(y, x, nullhyp = "qapy")` | `net_mrqap(y, x, method = "y")` | Y-permutation (Krackhardt 1988). |

Statistical models (ERGMs and stochastic actor-oriented models) are
planned.

## Conventions: what changes with `convention = "sna"`

On a simple network (no loops, no parallel edges) that is connected,
most measures agree whichever convention is used. They part ways in three
situations.

**Loops and parallel edges.** [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) reads an adjacency matrix, so two
recorded ties between the same pair are one tie, and a self-loop is a
diagonal cell it ignores. [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), and knappnet's default count
every edge:

```{r}
multi <- net_frame(data.frame(source = c("a", "a", "b", "c"),
                             target   = c("b", "b", "c", "c")), directed = FALSE)
data.frame(node = multi$nodes$id,
           default = net_degree(multi),
           sna = net_degree(multi, convention = "sna"))
```

**Disconnected networks.** sna's closeness is 0 for any node that cannot
reach every other node. With the Pucci isolate in the network, that is
every family:

```{r}
sna_closeness <- sna::closeness(m, gmode = "graph", cmode = "undirected")
data.frame(family = flo$nodes$name,
           sna = sna_closeness,
           knappnet_sna = net_closeness(flo, convention = "sna"),
           knappnet_default = round(net_closeness(flo, normalized = TRUE), 3))
```

The default (igraph's convention) uses only the nodes each node can
reach. Harmonic centrality, `net_harmonic()`, avoids the problem
altogether, and with `convention = "sna"` it is sna's
`cmode = "suminvundir"`.

**Centralization maxima.** sna and igraph divide by different theoretical
maxima for degree centralization; in a star, sna's index is 1 and igraph's
default is lower, because igraph's maximum allows for self-loops:

```{r}
star <- net_frame(data.frame(source = "hub", target = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e")),
                 directed = FALSE)
c(igraph = net_centralization(star, "degree"),
  sna = net_centralization(star, "degree", convention = "sna"),
  sna_itself = sna::centralization(as.matrix(star), sna::degree, mode = "graph",
                                   cmode = "indegree"))
```

## Node-level measures agree

```{r}
sna_scores <- data.frame(
  degree      = sna::degree(m, gmode = "graph", cmode = "indegree"),
  betweenness = sna::betweenness(m, gmode = "graph", cmode = "undirected"),
  harmonic    = sna::closeness(m, gmode = "graph", cmode = "suminvundir")
)
kn_scores <- data.frame(
  degree      = net_degree(flo, convention = "sna"),
  betweenness = net_betweenness(flo, convention = "sna"),
  harmonic    = net_harmonic(flo, convention = "sna")
)
sapply(names(sna_scores), function(v) {
  isTRUE(all.equal(kn_scores[[v]], sna_scores[[v]], check.attributes = FALSE))
})
```

Brokerage counts match [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna)'s `raw.nli`, column for column. Here the
families are split into two arbitrary groups:

```{r}
side <- ifelse(flo$nodes$name < "M", 1, 2)   # A-L and M-Z
kn_brokerage <- net_brokerage(flo, side)
sna_brokerage <- sna::brokerage(m, side)$raw.nli[, c("w_I", "w_O", "b_IO", "b_OI", "b_O", "t")]
all.equal(unname(as.matrix(kn_brokerage[, -1])), unname(sna_brokerage))
```

So do structural equivalence distances:

```{r}
all.equal(unname(net_struct_equiv(flo, "hamming")),
          unname(as.matrix(sna::sedist(m, method = "hamming"))))
```

## QAP: `net_qap_cor()` and `net_mrqap()` against `qaptest()` and `netlm()`

The quadratic assignment procedure tests dyadic hypotheses by permuting
node labels (Krackhardt 1987, 1988). Here, in a small office, we ask
whether advice ties follow friendship or department lines:

```{r}
staff <- data.frame(
  id = c("ann", "bob", "cat", "dan", "eve", "fay"),
  dept = c("sales", "sales", "eng", "eng", "eng", "legal")
)
advice <- net_frame(
  data.frame(source = c("ann", "bob", "cat", "dan", "eve", "bob", "fay", "ann"),
             target   = c("bob", "cat", "dan", "eve", "cat", "fay", "dan", "cat")),
  nodes = staff
)
friends <- net_frame(
  data.frame(source = c("ann", "ann", "bob", "cat", "dan"),
             target   = c("bob", "eve", "eve", "fay", "eve")),
  nodes = staff, directed = FALSE
)
same_dept <- outer(staff$dept, staff$dept, "==") * 1

Y <- as.matrix(advice)
X <- as.matrix(friends)
```

`net_qap_cor()` and `net_mrqap()` accept net_frames, matrices, or a mix. The
statistics themselves are identical to [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna)'s:

```{r}
test <- net_qap_cor(advice, friends, exact = TRUE)
c(knappnet = test$statistic, sna = sna::gcor(Y, X))

fit <- net_mrqap(advice, list(friends = friends, same_dept = same_dept), exact = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
sna_fit <- sna::netlm(Y, list(X, same_dept), reps = 1000)
rbind(knappnet = fit$coefficients, sna = sna_fit$coefficients)
```

The p-values estimate the same quantities. sna draws random
permutations; with six people there are only 6! = 720 relabelings, so
`exact = TRUE` evaluates every one of them and the p-values are exact.
sna's Monte Carlo estimates scatter around them:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sna_test <- sna::qaptest(list(Y, X), sna::gcor, g1 = 1, g2 = 2, reps = 1000)
rbind(knappnet_exact = test$p.value[c("Pr(<=r)", "Pr(>=r)")],
      sna_1000_draws = c(sna_test$pleeq, sna_test$pgreq))

rbind(knappnet_exact = fit$p.value[, "Pr(>=|b|)"],
      sna_1000_draws = sna_fit$pgreqabs)
```

Two details make results line up:

- **Dyads.** `mode = "digraph"` (the default) uses every ordered pair of
  distinct nodes and `mode = "graph"` each unordered pair once, from the
  lower triangle; `diag = TRUE` adds the diagonal. These are `gcor()` and
  `netlm()`'s conventions. An undirected net_frame gives a symmetric
  matrix, for which `mode = "graph"` is appropriate.
- **p-values.** As in sna, the observed statistic is not counted among
  the draws. `(test$counts + 1) / (test$valid + 1)` gives the form that
  counts it (Phipson and Smyth 2010), which is never zero.

Randomized runs take a `seed` (or draw one from R's generator, so
`set.seed()` works) and give the same answer with any number of threads.
Missing values are handled by listwise deletion of dyads, as in sna; see
`?qap_cor` and `?mrqap` for the details, including the one case (missing
values in a predictor under double semi-partialling) where sna's results
are not comparable.
